STAGE.tell: Imperative stage direction to the reader
STAGE.why: Telling the reader to read it again, sit with it, mark it or hold it is a performance cue. It recurs across the library in the same shape, which is how a reader spots the machine. The fact that follows carries the weight without the cue.
STAGE.note: Short imperatives aimed at the reader, usually as a paragraph opener: Read that again, Sit with that, Mark that, Note what that means, Hold both, Be fair to, Say it plainly, Name it, Count, Measure. 48 of them, 11 in the-attractional-era alone. One or two would be his voice. Forty-eight is a tic, and it is the single most recognisable machine rhythm in the four long modern essays.

HONEST.why: The brief allows one use per essay. The library uses honest/honesty 57 times and 'fair/fairly/fairness' as a framing device in most essays. Prose that keeps certifying its own honesty reads as generated.
HONEST.note: "Honest", "honesty" and "honestly" appear 57 times; "honesty requires", "honesty says so", "honesty forbids" and "honesty keeps" recur as a formula. "Fair", "fairly" and "fairness" do the same job in the-counter-reformation, the-long-middle and awakenings-and-enlightenment. Four subtitles and two section titles certify the essay's own honesty. After the fixes 19 uses remain, nearly all of them describing someone else.

CLOSER.tell: Aphoristic closer, fragment stack or symmetrical pair
CLOSER.why: A two-beat epigram or a stack of fragments at the end of a paragraph. The governing standard asks for one earned verdict and developed sentences, and puts perfect parallelism on the avoid list. These land in nearly every section of the longer essays.
CLOSER.note: Two-beat epigrams, mirror-image sentence pairs and fragment stacks at paragraph ends. The four dash-heavy essays close nearly every section this way; the long modern essays do it every third paragraph. The findings keep the one line per section that the argument has earned and fold or cut the rest.

TURN.why: 'Here is the...', 'Now the...', 'And then the...' announce a move instead of making it. The brief lists these among the tells earlier judges caught.
TURN.note: "Here is the...", "Now the...", "And then the...", "One more fact, and it must not be softened". Each announces a move the next sentence makes anyway. Plain signposting ("This essay tells how that happened") is his habit and was left alone.

FLAT.why: This sentence could sit in any church-history handout. No contraction where speech would have one, a 'We should...' opener, or a question written as a statement.
FLAT.note: Four short essays (the-apostolic-age, the-great-councils, the-east-west-schism, the-reformation) have the opposite problem from the rest. They carry no dashes and almost no slogans, and also no person. the-apostolic-age has zero contractions in 1,341 words; four questions across these essays are punctuated as statements; "We should..." and "We should not pretend..." open paragraph after paragraph. They read as competent handouts that any church could post unchanged.

STOCK.tell: Stock line or motif reused across essays
STOCK.why: The same sentence or image appears in more than one essay in the library. Read together, the repetition shows.
STOCK.note: The accounting metaphor (ledger, bill, invoice, receipt, audit, price tag, tuition) appears 40 times across fourteen essays and supplies three kickers and two titles. Other repeats: "what you win them with is what you win them to" (two essays), "one ordinary Tuesday at a time" (two endings), Rome "collecting gods the way it collected provinces" (two essays), "the whole era is folded inside it" (two essays), "lived inside that sentence / that answer" (two essays), "no modern consultant would fund / recognize" (two essays).

HEADING.tell: Literary heading or kicker where a plain one belongs
HEADING.why: The brief asks for plain descriptive headings. A reader scanning the page should learn what the section covers.
HEADING.note: Most section titles are plain and good ("What Rome Actually Wanted", "Was Constantine Sincere", "What Made Luther Possible"). These are the ones that are literary or clever instead.

PARADE.why: 'In YEAR the historian X published TITLE' repeated through one essay is the scholar parade the brief names. The year already sits in the key-figures list.
PARADE.note: Mild, and confined to after-christendom-era, where three sources are introduced with the same year-and-title formula. In the library as a whole the named scholars do real work (Hatch, Noll, Stout, Bebbington, Kreider, Walls, Sanneh each carry an idea), which is a strength.

CARE.tell: Crisis-facing passage with no path to help
CARE.why: The section describes abuse by church leaders. The integrity rules ask that such a passage say abuse should be reported to the authorities and keep help visible.

how_to_apply: Each finding names a file, a field (subtitle | section.title | section.kicker | section.body | keyFigures.note) and a key (the section id, or the key figure's name). Within that field the quote occurs exactly once; replace it with the replacement (an empty replacement means delete the quoted words). Findings do not overlap, so order does not matter. Newlines in a quote are literal \n\n paragraph breaks in the body string. After applying, the library contains no em-dashes or en-dashes.
